case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload

3 = Moderate workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics.   genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Case:
A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

  A. Ask about low back pain and order HLA-B27 testing
  B. Ask about oral ulcers and perform fluorescein angiography
  C. Ask about tattoos and order chest computed tomography to evaluate for lymphadenopathy
  D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

Case:
A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

  A. Ask about low back pain and order HLA-B27 testing
  B. Ask about oral ulcers and perform fluorescein angiography
  C. Ask about tattoos and order chest computed tomography to evaluate for lymphadenopathy
  D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.
